READING 47
INDUSTRY AND COMPETITIVE
ANALYSIS
MODULE 47.1: INDUSTRY ANALYSIS
FRAMEWORK
LOS 47.a: Describe the process of industry and competitive analysis.
Analysts conduct industry and competitive analysis to assess the environment in
which a company operates. An industry, in this context, is a group of firms that
offers comparable products or services. By evaluating the drivers of an
industry’s size and profits, an analyst can clearly explain the rationale behind the
inputs in valuation models and the narrative that shapes and supports these
inputs.
PROFESSOR’S NOTE
As we will see in the Ethical and Professional Standards topic area,
being able to explain these things helps an analyst demonstrate that an
investment recommendation has a reasonable basis.
Conducting industry and competitive analysis involves five steps:
Step 1:    Define the industry in terms of its scope, which is often subjective.
This requires identifying the factors that define an industry (e.g., product
similarity or geographical region) and deciding how to treat companies
that operate in multiple industries. Classification systems produced by
third parties provide standardized guidance.
Step 2:    Survey the industry in terms of its size, growth rate, profitability, and
composition.
Step 3:    Analyze the industry structure using a framework such as Porter’s five
forces to determine the degree of competitive rivalry and key profitability

drivers.
Step 4:    Examine external influences using a framework such as PESTLE:
political, economic, social, technological, legal, and environmental
influences.
Step 5:    Analyze companies’ competitive strategies in terms of how each
company fits within the industry and what competitive advantages each
company has.
LOS 47.b: Describe industry classification methods and compare methods
by which companies can be grouped.
The first step in industry and competitive analysis is to define the company’s
industry. Industries are composed of firms with common competitive forces and
value drivers. Once a company has been classified into an industry, an analyst
can search for peers against which to compare the company.
Commercial or Third-Party Classification Systems
One way to determine how to classify a company is to consult a commercial, or
third-party, classification service. These global organizations independently
assess the products and services offered by companies and classify those that are
similar, according to hierarchical taxonomies. The lowest tier, where the
company sits, is a single group; higher tiers are aggregate groups. Widely used
classification systems include:
Global Industry Classification Standard (GICS). This was developed by S&P
Dow Jones Indices and MSCI for public companies. It classifies by sector,
industry groups, industries, and subindustries.
Industry Classification Benchmark (ICB). This was developed by FTSE
Russell for public companies. It classifies by industries, supersectors, sectors,
and subsectors.
The Refinitiv Business Classification (TRBC). This was developed by Refinitiv
for public companies, private companies, not-for-profits, and government
entities. It classifies by economic sectors, business sectors, industry groups,
industries, and activities.
These third-party providers review and update their classifications annually at a
minimum, with some adding new companies to their offerings more frequently.

In addition to these global organizations, regional systems that provide
classifications include the North American Industry Classification System
(NAICS) and the European Nomenclature of Economic Activities (NACE).
Data providers such as Bloomberg, FactSet, and S&P Capital IQ, as well as
stock exchanges such as the Nasdaq, either use these industry classification
systems or construct their own similar taxonomies.
The primary advantage of using a commercial classification system is its
consistency. However, these systems have limitations. The classifications may be
too broad or too narrow and often require some judgment.
Industry groupings can include companies with different business models or
substitute products. For example, McDonald’s Corporation (MCD) and Yum!
Brands, Inc. (YUM) are classified under the GICS Restaurant subindustry, but
McDonald’s owns a significant franchisee real estate portfolio, which some
analysts believe should be valued separately for better comparison.
Companies might operate in multiple industries. Some classification systems
with strict taxonomies classify companies based on the product or service that
generates the most revenue. Not all systems follow the same guidelines, which
can cause problems when attempting to make comparisons. For example, some
systems assign Amazon to the “consumer discretionary retailer” industry
despite its significant growth in cloud computing.
Industries may have different constituents due to geographical differences.
These include health care or insurance companies, which cannot operate on a
global basis. These industries may be less easy to compare using the
taxonomies of the major third-party providers. Regulations, cultural behavior,
or shipping costs may also make global taxonomies impractical.
Groupings shift or evolve over time. Groupings that shift or evolve over time
to reflect natural business changes may undergo reclassification. For example,
in 2023, GICS moved two companies, Visa and Mastercard, to the “transaction
and payments processing services” classification in the financial sector (from
the data processing industry within the information technology sector). Other
examples of evolution include industries with new entrants, or delistings
resulting from acquisitions and bankruptcies. To account for these types of
changes, analysts may need to restate historical data to ensure that the current
groupings are comparable.

Classification by Geography
Classification systems can be based on a company’s country of domicile.
Countries are, in turn, categorized by level of industrialization, such as
developed, emerging, or frontier economies. The country used for classification
is most often where a company is headquartered or listed on an exchange, even
if it does most of its business elsewhere. For example, Toyota is considered a
Japanese company, but it generates most of its revenues in North America.
Analysts should be aware that a company’s geographic classification might not
reflect its revenue profile or the location of its assets.
Classification by Business Cycle Sensitivity
Depending on the degree to which economic fluctuations affect their revenue
and profitability, companies can be classified as defensive, cyclical, or growth.
A defensive company produces goods and services with relatively stable
demand over the business cycle. Defensive sectors include health care, utilities,
telecommunications, and consumer staples. Those sectors produce items
required for day-to-day living, the demand for which is not affected significantly
by fluctuations in macroeconomic activity.
A cyclical company is one whose earnings are highly dependent on the stage of
the business cycle. Such companies have high earnings volatility and typically
high operating leverage. Their products often have long lifespans, such as
materials or equipment sold to other producers; or high-unit-value items whose
purchase can be delayed until the economy improves, such as automobiles or
home appliances. The commodities that serve as inputs for these products also
vary with demand. Fluctuating revenue and high fixed costs can result in volatile
operating profits. Examples of cyclical industries include basic materials and
processing, consumer discretionary, energy, financial services, and industrial and
producer durables.
PROFESSOR’S NOTE
The curriculum learning module omits telecommunications from
defensive companies and energy and producer durables from cyclical
companies. We include them here for completeness.
A growth company typically demonstrates strong revenue growth through all
cycles. These companies may or may not be profitable, depending on which

phase of the company life cycle characterizes them. When evaluating growth
companies, analysts should try to determine how long growth will remain above
trend and, as growth plateaus, what the profit levels are likely to be in the
industry. Growth companies are often in industries such as emerging technology
or biotechnology.
When an analyst covers companies in countries that vary with respect to their
positions in the business cycle, combining business cycle sensitivity with
geography to classify companies may be appropriate.
LOS 47.c: Determine an industry’s size, growth characteristics,
profitability, and market share trends.
The second step in industry and competitive analysis is to survey the industry to
gauge its size, historical rate of growth, growth drivers, profitability, and key
constituents and their market share trends.
Industry Size
Industry size is the total annual sales of the product or service under
consideration. This is not always the same as total annual sales of all the
companies in the industry. For companies that operate in multiple product lines,
only the relevant portion of their total annual sales should be included in
industry size.
Figure 47.1 describes two approaches to estimating industry size: top down and
bottom up.
Figure 47.1: Approaches to Estimating Industry Size

Industry Growth Characteristics
Industry growth should be evaluated against broad measures of economic
activity to determine an industry’s life cycle stage, and over the business cycle to
determine its sensitivity to fluctuations in the economy.
Growth industries typically expand faster than the general economy no matter
what the stage of the business cycle because they have not yet reached all of
their total addressable market. Analysts must judge the persistence of high
growth rates and estimate when they will peak. This is more problematic when
an industry’s growth is based on an emerging technology.
Mature industries have little or no growth potential remaining in their markets.
Given that the growth rate of all industries combined should equal the rate of
economic growth, maturing industries should grow near or below the rate of the
economy. Analysts should focus on any disruptors, such as significant changes
in the intensity of competition among industry participants, as well as any signs
that the industry might be declining overall.
Business cycle sensitivity is an additional consideration. Industries exposed to
interest rate movements or those involving discretionary sales or capital goods
experience more revenue volatility over a business cycle.
Structural changes, such as those that occurred during the COVID-19 pandemic,
may also affect industry demand, and they need to be factored into any analysis.

Industry Profitability
Industry profitability is commonly measured using operating profit margin or
return on invested capital (ROIC):
ROIC measures value creation across all investments and can be compared to a
company’s weighted average cost of capital (WACC). When ROIC > WACC, the
company is providing a positive return.
Unfortunately, it is often impractical to estimate ROIC for private companies
that do not have publicly available financial statements. Instead, analysts may
use the returns of publicly traded companies and assume they are similar for
private companies, or they may use data provided by a government or a third-
party provider.
Market Share
Another key component of the industry survey is to determine market share for
each company within the industry. Over a specified period, market share is
calculated as follows:
Because industry size is difficult to measure, market share should be estimated
as a range instead of a specific point.
The trend in a company’s market share over time helps determine whether
customers view its products favorably. By tracking market share changes over
time, an analyst can also detect increased competition from new entrants to the
market. Conversely, industry consolidation may increase a company’s market
share, and an analyst should determine whether a company is increasing its
market share net of acquisitions.
Unless an industry is segmented or has a high degree of product differentiation,

greater industry concentration indicates less competition, and less industry
concentration suggests more competition. An analyst can gauge industry
concentration using the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI). The HHI is the
sum of the squares of the market shares of all industry participants.
For example, a market consisting of five companies, with shares of 35%, 25%,
20%, 10%, and 10%, would have an HHI of 352 + 252 + 202 + 102 + 102 =
2,450.
The maximum HHI is 1002 or 10,000, which would indicate that a company is a
monopoly. In some countries, regulators use HHI to determine which industries
require closer scrutiny. An HHI greater than 1,800 is often interpreted to indicate
high concentration.
MODULE QUIZ 47.1
1. Industry classification systems from commercial index providers typically classify firms by:
A. statistical methods.
B. products and services.
C. business cycle sensitivity.
2. Firms and industries are most appropriately classified as cyclical or noncyclical based on:
A. their stock price fluctuations relative to the market.
B. the sensitivity of their earnings to the business cycle.
C. the volatility of their earnings relative to their competitors.
3. A pet food company earned $500 million in revenue in the current year. Based on an
estimated market share of 10%, what is the market size for pet food?
A. $0.5 billion.
B. $4.5 billion.
C. $5.0 billion.
MODULE 47.2: PORTER’S FIVE FORCES AND
PESTLE ANALYSIS
LOS 47.d: Analyze an industry’s structure and external influences using
Porter’s Five Forces and the PESTLE framework.
The third step in industry and competitive analysis is to examine the industry’s
structure and the competitive rivalry within it.

The analytical framework developed by Michael Porter1 describes industry
competitive forces that determine long-run profitability. If some or all the forces
he described are strong, industry return on capital is unlikely to exceed the cost
of capital. Conversely, if the forces are less intense, industry profitability should
be high.
To illustrate the concept of competitive advantage Porter discussed, Warren
Buffet coined the phrase economic moat. Like the water that protected castles
from invaders, an economic moat shields company profits from competitors. The
longer a company can maintain its competitive advantage, the wider its
economic moat, and the longer its profit will remain above its capital costs.
Some examples of factors that contribute to an economic moat are production
cost advantages, the ability to operate at an efficient scale, ownership of
proprietary intangible assets, network effects from using a company’s products,
and high switching costs for customers.
In an industry with few competitors, such as an oligopoly, all companies have
wide moats. In more competitive industries, fewer companies have wide moats,
while most generate returns below their cost of capital.
To evaluate competitive rivalry within an industry, analysts can compare
Porter’s five forces with the factors that determine the width of a company’s
economic moat:
Threat of new entrants. Both the number of new entrants over time and their
industry impact are important to consider when assessing market share. To
address the threat posed by new rivals, a company may rely on the following
courses of action:
Partner with or acquire new rivals to mitigate their impact.
Lobby for government regulation that restricts entry into an industry, or for
government subsidies for domestic companies.
Support restrictive licensing requirements so that the cost of complying with
government regulation is a barrier to entry.
File for patents that grant their holders exclusive rights to their products or
technologies for numerous years.
Develop intangible assets, such as customer loyalty.
Increase retention by emphasizing the high costs of switching, which include
the price, opportunity cost, transition risk, and missed opportunity to receive

upgrades from the existing provider.
Leverage network effects to solidify market dominance as user adoption
grows and enhances product value.
Pursue cost advantages. These may coincide with other sources of
competitive advantage such as scale, brand loyalty, proprietary technology, or
economies of scope (when the cost of producing a combination of goods and
services is less than producing each separately). Mature industries with
inelastic demand for commoditized products must operate at an efficient
scale. The fact that new entrants would potentially push returns in these
industries below the cost of capital acts as a barrier to entry.
Threat of substitutes. Goods and services that address the same needs as an
existing product limit the profit potential of an industry by increasing the
elasticity of demand. These substitute products, in turn, limit the prices firms
can charge. Substitutes may come from seemingly different industries and shift
consumer norms, much like videoconferencing software has changed the
landscape for workers and become a substitute for physical office space.
Bargaining power of suppliers. Suppliers’ ability to raise prices or limit supply
influences industry profitability. Suppliers are more powerful if just a few of
them exist, if their products are scarce or customized, or if switching costs are
high. For example, Microsoft is one of the few suppliers of operating system
software, so it has pricing power. Supplier bargaining power may also be
exerted through proprietary technology licenses, intellectual property, or
specialized and highly skilled labor, including labor that requires licensing or is
well organized. By contrast, supplier bargaining power is weak when there are
many small-scale providers of commoditized goods that have ready substitutes.
Bargaining power of customers. Buyers’ ability to bargain for lower prices or
higher quality influences industry profitability. For example, bargaining by
governments and ever-larger health care providers have put downward pressure
even on patented drugs. Customers tend to have greater power when they are a
large and concentrated base, when products are more commodity-like, or when
switching costs are low. In these cases, customers may influence payment
terms, pricing, quality standards, and delivery times. In response, companies
may reward customer loyalty, bundle services, or differentiate their products.
Companies looking to mitigate the effects of external bargaining power may
pursue vertical integration, expanding their operations to an earlier stage of
production (upstream or backward integration) or a later stage (downstream or

forward integration) to control more of the delivery process. Companies can
also participate in joint ventures or exclusive supplier agreements, or they can
eliminate intermediaries.
Rivalry among existing competitors. Rivalry may manifest as price
competition, product differentiation, market share changes, or changes in
industry growth or profitability. Slow growth leads to competition as firms fight
for market share, and high fixed costs lead to price decreases as firms try to
operate at full capacity.
EXAMPLE: Porter’s five forces analysis for the passenger airline industry2
Threat of New Entrants: Low to Moderate
Potential entrants in the passenger airline industry face significant capital
investment requirements, with industry incumbents benefiting from economies
of scale. Such regulatory hurdles as strict aviation regulations, licensing
requirements, and even barriers to exit in some markets serve as deterrents to
new industry entrants.
While established global airlines benefit from extensive networks and frequent
flyer programs, in some regions or markets, low-cost carriers (LCCs) have a
lower entry barrier due to flexible leasing options, limited schedules, and the
use of secondary airports. As a result, the threat of entry is low for major
global carriers but moderate for LCCs in many regional and underserved
markets.
Threat of Substitutes: Moderate
While driving and high-speed rail travel represent substitutes for short-haul
passenger air travel, long-haul flights have few alternatives. Business-related
travel remains affected by remote work trends and virtual meetings, as
described in an earlier example. However, few alternatives to air transportation
exist for leisure travel and tourism. As a result, substitutes for passenger air
travel are a moderate threat and are more pronounced for shorter trips and
business-related travel, while longer flights and leisure travel are less
susceptible to substitution.
Bargaining Power of Suppliers: High
Passenger airline companies are dependent on aircraft manufacturers, fuel
deliveries, and unionized employees as key suppliers. The global dominance of
jet aircraft manufacturers Boeing and Airbus leave airlines with little

bargaining power. As a major expense item for passenger airlines, oil prices are
subject to significant volatility, which affects operating margins. Airline pilots,
engineers, and maintenance workers are often well organized; this affords them
the ability to negotiate wage and benefit increases, driving up airline operating
expenses. Airlines are heavily dependent on these suppliers, which have strong
bargaining power due to their critical role in operations and the lack of
substitutes.
Bargaining Power of Customers: High
Passenger airline customers are very sensitive to price differences, which are
highly transparent given the widespread practice of online travel booking.
While airlines use such strategies as branded credit cards, frequent flyer
programs, premium seating, and travel lounge access, customer loyalty is
limited, given low switching costs—particularly for short-haul trips and
popular destinations.
Demand for non-essential air travel is also sensitive to the business cycle.
Business travelers may face constraints due to restrictive travel policies, limit
travel in economic downturns, and may forgo travel altogether in favor of
remote meetings as described earlier. Leisure travelers may delay discretionary
holiday travel or substitute ground travel for flights when seeking to limit
expenses. As a result, customer bargaining power in the passenger airline
industry is considered high.
Rivalry Among Existing Competitors: High
A high degree of industry rivalry results from numerous global and regional
airlines and LCCs competing on price, routes, and service quality while facing
high operating expenses and suppliers with significant bargaining power.
Regulatory constraints limit the degree of industry consolidation, while
limitations on reducing capacity during economic downturns leads to greater
price competition. As illustrated in an earlier example, the airline industry
faces cyclical demand and returns below the cost of capital over the cycle,
intensifying the rivalry among competitors.
PESTLE Analysis
The fourth step in industry and competitive analysis is to examine the industry’s
external influences. The PESTLE framework identifies external influences as
political, economic, social, technological, legal, and environmental factors.

Political influences have an important and widespread effect on businesses
through various channels, including taxes, subsidies, and reimbursements.
Influences may be indirect (e.g., changes in monetary policy, regulation, and
geopolitical factors) or direct (e.g., a government purchase of an industry’s
products or services). Sectors that are notably exposed to political influences
include energy, health care, and defense.
Economic influences can be cyclical trends in economic output or structural
changes, such as an economy’s competitiveness and stage of development. For
example, capital investment in a developing country may increase labor
productivity and lift its growth rate above those of developed countries. In
conducting industry and competitive analysis, an industry’s expected
performance should align with economic forecasts after adjusting for its stage in
the business cycle. Exchange rates also play a role in industry growth as they
affect the costs and competitiveness of goods in other markets. A depreciating
currency boosts exports, while a strengthening currency makes imports cheaper
for domestic buyers.
Social influences relate to trends in how people work, play, spend their money,
and conduct their lives. These factors are particularly important for industries
that sell directly to individuals. At times, these trends evolve with economic
change, such as a shift away from low-cost goods to brand-name products as
income levels rise. For more affluent consumers, quality, brand image, and
features such as flexibility, convenience, or health consciousness become
increasingly important. Some companies are bowing to pressures to use socially
responsible procurement of raw materials, and to ensure that production
processes are ethical and observe human rights.
Technological influences can change an industry dramatically through the
introduction of new or improved products or services that can make existing
ones redundant. Technology change is key to total factor productivity within an
industry and in the overall economy.
To assess the impact of technology advancement on industry competition,
innovations can be classified according to their domain (i.e., the products,
market segments, or business processes they affect) and the problems they are
meant to solve. An innovation matrix, as shown in Figure 47.2, categorizes
innovations into four categories: basic research, breakthrough innovation,
sustaining innovation, and disruptive innovation.

Figure 47.2: Innovation Matrix3
. Basic research. This is indistinct in terms of its domain and the problem, and
it deepens the understanding of scientific principles without a specific
commercial objective.
. Breakthrough innovation. This has an indistinct domain and a distinct
problem, and it introduces a new product, service, or business model that has
significant impact across industries. An example is the rechargeable lithium
battery used in smartphones, computers, and cars.
. Sustaining innovation. This focuses on distinct problems within distinct
domains, such as feature enhancements that improve functionality.
. Disruptive innovation. This focuses on indistinct problems within distinct
domains; it creates new markets or redefines existing markets. An example is
the introduction of streaming services that have surpassed cable subscriptions.
When markets are disrupted, companies can either change their business
models or adapt more slowly and lose market share.
Legal influences consider changes in laws and regulations that present both
business risks and opportunities. Consider the tobacco industry, which has faced
declining revenues due to laws implemented in many jurisdictions over the past
few decades, such as prohibiting smoking in public places and requiring
extensive disclosures on cigarette packages. In contrast, consider the relatively
new cannabis industry that has developed in jurisdictions that have legalized its
sale and use.
Environmental influences, such as climate change and concerns about
environmental sustainability of some industries, are often connected with
political, social, and legal influences. The energy industry is often challenged to
address environmental concerns. Many in the industry are grappling with the

energy transition, which is a government-mandated structural shift to reduce the
emission of greenhouse gases through policy, taxes, and subsidies.
Analyzing individual companies within an industry, the fifth step in industry and
competitive analysis, will be discussed in the next reading.
MODULE QUIZ 47.2
1. Two of the five competitive forces in the Porter framework are:
A. threat of entry and barriers to exit.
B. power of suppliers and threat of substitutes.
C. rivalry among competitors and power of regulators.
2. Assessing the impact on an industry of the economic outlook is best described as an
example of:
A. surveying the industry.
B. analyzing the industry structure.
C. examining external influences.
KEY CONCEPTS
LOS 47.a
Industry and competitive analysis involves five steps:
Step 1:    Define the industry.
Step 2:    Survey the industry’s size, growth, profitability, and market share
trends.
Step 3:    Analyze the industry’s structure.
Step 4:    Analyze external influences on the industry.
Step 5:    Determine industry participants’ competitive strategies.
LOS 47.b
Three commercial classification systems and their hierarchical structures (four or
five tiers) are as follows:
GICS: sector, industry groups, industries, subindustries
ICB: industries, supersectors, sectors, subsectors
TRBC: economic sectors, business sectors, industry groups, industries,
activities

Limitations of classification systems include inappropriate groupings with
companies with different business models or substitute products; inaccurate
classifications of companies selling multiple products; the inability to deal with
products and services offered in local or national markets only; and groupings
that change over time.
Other ways to group companies include geography, business cycle sensitivity, or
a combination of these two approaches.
LOS 47.c
Industry size is the total annual sales of the product, which is not always the
same as total annual sales of all the companies in the industry.
A top-down approach to evaluating industry size uses data from a government
agency or third-party provider. A bottom-up approach involves adding the
revenue from all the companies that produce the goods or services in question.
Growth industries expand faster than the general economy. Mature industries
have growth rates that are in line with the general economy or decreasing.
Industry profitability is commonly measured as follows:
Market share is a company’s annual revenues as a percentage of the industry
total sales.
Industry concentration is often expressed numerically using the Herfindahl-
Hirschman Index (HHI), the sum of the squares of the market shares of all
industry participants.
LOS 47.d
Porter’s five forces that determine industry competition are as follows:
Threat of new entrants
Threat of substitutes
Bargaining power of customers
Bargaining power of suppliers
Rivalry among existing competitors

PESTLE analysis consists of six elements:
Political influences
Economic influences
Social influences
Technology influences
Legal influences
Environmental influences
